title: Education's dark matter
author: Ashman, Greg
summary: Greg Ashman argues that education is more like physics than biology: most of what teachers do daily is not evidence-based and probably never can be, because most classroom decisions fall into dark matter—territory that hasn't been and can't be empirically studied in any meaningful way. This doesn't justify educational relativism, but it does mean the honest position is 'evidence-informed' rather than 'evidence-based,' and that craft knowledge, rightly understood, is irreplaceable in teaching.
points: Most daily teaching decisions fall into education's dark matter—areas with no direct research evidence—making pure evidence-based practice impossible and craft knowledge indispensable.
The correct position is evidence-informed rather than evidence-based: where evidence exists, educators have a responsibility to use it; where it doesn't, wisdom and craft must guide.
Claims of far transfer—that training in one subject improves outcomes in unrelated fields—have repeatedly failed to replicate, undermining grand empirical claims in education.
Positivism, the view that only empirical evidence matters, is impossible to implement in a school: leaders without values and judgment cannot run an institution.
VCE rankings and similar data are largely indices of socioeconomic status rather than educational quality, but once numbers appear in spreadsheets they acquire unwarranted authority.
The gap between what a small laboratory study can tell us and the complexity of real teaching decisions means most classroom practice will always be craft-based, not algorithm-based.
quotes: Sometimes these studies are indeed conducted in education faculties in actual laboratory settings, but more often, like my research, they take place in schools and universities and they mostly target educationally relevant objectives.

We can draw tentative inferences from, say, the effectiveness of cognitive behavioural therapy and so align a school’s approach around Stoic principles, but we can never really know whether that is valid.
The difference between my position and that of education academics who take a relativist stance is that where evidence does exist, I believe we have a responsibility to be informed by it.
There is no independent way of checking and so the VCE ranking that is published every December does not tell us much and is more an index of socioeconomic status than anything else.
We have large and expanding numbers of students doing challenging subjects such as mathematical methods, chemistry, physics and so on, but you would have to take my word for it.
It may be able to tell us one small thing about presenting information to students, but that will inform one decision out of the many a teacher makes when planning a lesson.
